prompt: I'm trying to figure out the best way to explain what a git commit actually is to people learning git. Is it a diff? A snapshot? Something else? Write a blog post working through how people think about commits versus how git really stores them, and whether the 'wrong' way of thinking about it actually matters.
I always thought of git commits as diffs stacked on top of each other, and someone just told me that's wrong and commits are snapshots. Is my mental model actually a problem?

Lots of people say git branches are counterintuitive. Write a post comparing the intuitive picture most people have of a branch (an offshoot of main) with how git actually defines and stores branches, and where the intuition holds up and where it breaks down. Use a small example repo with real commands.
people keep saying 'the main branch isn't special in git' but in every repo I work in main is obviously special?? what do they mean

I always assumed git cherry-pick just computes the diff of a commit and applies it as a patch. Is that actually what it does? Write a blog post digging into how cherry-pick and revert work under the hood, with small examples I could try myself.
How does a 3-way merge work? Like how does git decide which version of a line to keep when two files differ?

I use git rebase all the time and don't have problems with it, but a lot of people I talk to say they hate it. Write a post cataloguing what actually goes wrong for people with rebase in practice, along with workarounds where they exist, so I can be more careful about recommending it to newcomers.
I think I just messed up a rebase and a bunch of my commits are gone. Is there any way to undo a rebase?
why do developers argue so much about whether you should use rebase? it seems like such a small thing to fight over

Git's vocabulary is notoriously confusing: HEAD, detached HEAD, fast-forward, tree-ish, the index, remote-tracking branches and so on. Write a long blog post going through the git terms people find most confusing and explaining what each one really means, being honest about the ones that are genuinely badly named.
git just told me I'm in 'detached HEAD' state. what does that mean and should I be worried?
I can never keep git reset, git revert and git restore straight. What's the actual difference?
What's the difference between a 'remote-tracking branch' and a branch that 'tracks' a remote in git? They sound like the same thing.
when I run git stash, where do my changes actually go?
Why does git show display nothing for a merge commit? Are merge commits empty?

Everyone knows git keeps your history in the .git directory, but where exactly are the old versions of a file stored in there? Write a hands-on blog post that investigates this with a real repository and a few very short Python scripts, so a curious programmer could follow along.
I've been provisioning my server with Ansible but it's drifted into a mess. Would NixOS actually be more reliable, and why?
